title: Foundation Cracks: Which Ones Are Harmless and Which Need a Pro
question: Is a crack in my foundation serious, and how do I fix it?
summary: Most foundation cracks are thin, vertical, and caused by concrete shrinking as it cured. They are not structural and only need sealing. Call a structural engineer if a crack is horizontal, wider than 1/4 inch, keeps growing, or has one side pushed out past the other, or if you also see a bowing wall, sticking doors, or sloping floors. Either way, fix the drainage first. Water against the wall causes most leaks and many new cracks.

commonCauses.cause: Shrinkage as the concrete cured. Poured walls lose water and shrink, which leaves thin vertical or slightly angled cracks. They often start at the corner of a basement window. They are cosmetic, though they can let water in.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The crack is vertical or close to it, hairline to about 1/16 inch wide, and both sides are flush. A US quarter is about 1/16 inch thick; if its edge will not slide in, the crack is narrower than that.

commonCauses.cause: Settling or heaving soil under the footing. Clay soil shrinks in drought and swells when wet, and poorly packed fill settles. This makes diagonal cracks in poured walls and stair-step cracks along the mortar joints of block or brick.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The crack is wider at one end than the other, or one side sits higher or sticks out past the other by 1/8 inch or more. Check for sticking doors and windows or sloping floors nearby.

commonCauses.cause: Water pressure from poor drainage. Downspouts that dump next to the wall, soil that slopes toward the house, or a high water table load the wall with wet soil and push water through any crack.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The crack leaks or looks damp during or after rain. Look outside for downspouts that end at the wall, overflowing gutters, or ground that slopes toward the house.

commonCauses.cause: Frost. In cold climates, wet soil that freezes against the wall or under a shallow footing pushes on the foundation.
commonCauses.quickCheck: Cracks appear or widen in winter and early spring, often in the upper part of the wall or at unheated garages and porches.

commonCauses.cause: Soil pressure pushing the wall in. This is the serious one. Heavy, wet, or frozen soil pushes a basement wall inward until it cracks horizontally, often near mid-height. Walls of hollow concrete block are the most at risk.
commonCauses.quickCheck: The crack runs sideways across the wall, or the wall bows inward when you hold a long level or a tight string against it. Stop and call a structural engineer.

fixes: Read the crack. Note which way it runs (vertical, diagonal, stair-step, or horizontal) and measure the widest point with a ruler or a crack width card. Check whether both sides are flush. A thin vertical crack with flush sides is almost always shrinkage.

Decide if it needs an engineer. Stop here and call a structural engineer if the crack is horizontal, wider than 1/4 inch, offset, growing, stair-stepped and wider at one end, or paired with a bowing wall, sticking doors, or sloping floors. An engineer tells you what is moving and what repair fits. A contractor who sells the repair is not a neutral judge.

Watch it for change. Mark each end of the crack with a pencil line and the date, and measure the width at one marked spot. Take a photo with a ruler in the frame. Check again after a few weeks, after heavy rain, and across a season. A plastic crack monitor glued across the crack shows small movement. A crack that stays the same is dormant. A crack that grows is active and needs an engineer.

Fix the water first. Clean the gutters. Extend downspouts so water lands at least 5 feet from the wall, the distance the building code sets for expansive soil. Regrade so the ground drops at least 6 inches in the first 10 feet away from the house, and slope patios and walks within 10 feet at least 2 percent away. This stops most leaks and slows new cracking.

Seal a dry, dormant crack in a poured concrete wall with an injection kit. Epoxy bonds the two sides of the crack back together and works best on a dry crack that is not moving. Polyurethane foam reacts with water and swells to fill the crack, so it is the better choice for a damp or leaking crack. It stays flexible and is a waterproofing repair, not a structural one.

To inject, clean loose material out of the crack face, glue the plastic ports along it about as far apart as the wall is thick (or as the kit says), and cover the crack between ports with the paste. Inject at the lowest port until resin shows at the next port up, cap it, and move up. Let it cure, then cut off the ports.

Do not inject a hollow concrete block wall. The resin runs into the hollow cores instead of filling the crack. For a thin, stable stair-step crack in block, repoint the mortar joints. For anything wider or growing, call an engineer.
Use hydraulic cement to plug an active leak or a hole. It sets in about 3 to 5 minutes, even against running water. It is rigid, so it will crack again if the wall is still moving.
Keep checking after the repair. Mark and date the ends of the sealed crack. If it cracks again, the wall is still moving. That calls for an engineer, not more sealant.

Do not seal over a structural crack and call it done. Patching a horizontal crack or a bowing wall hides the problem. Structural fixes are designed by an engineer and installed by a foundation contractor: carbon-fiber straps, wall anchors, steel braces, or piers under the footing.
diyVsPro: You can handle thin, dormant, vertical cracks in a poured wall yourself: fix the gutters, downspouts, and grading, then seal the crack with an epoxy or polyurethane injection kit. Call a licensed structural engineer for any horizontal crack, any bowing or leaning wall, cracks wider than 1/4 inch, cracks that are offset or growing, stair-step cracks in block that are wider at one end, or cracks with sticking doors, sloping floors, or a chimney pulling away. A foundation inspection costs about $400 to $750, and a full structural engineer report $500 to $3,000. That is small next to repairs that can pass $10,000. Get the engineer's report before you take bids, so contractors price the same repair.
typicalCostUSD: DIY injection or sealant kit: $20-$80. Downspout extensions and grading materials: $50-$300. Professional crack injection: $250-$800 per crack. Foundation inspection: $400-$750; structural engineer report: $500-$3,000. Bowed wall repair (anchors, carbon-fiber straps, tiebacks): $5,000-$15,000. Underpinning with piers: $10,000-$30,000 or more.
timeEstimate: Reading and measuring the crack: 30 minutes. Sealing one crack with an injection kit: 1-2 hours plus cure time. Gutter, downspout, and grading work: half a day to a full day. Watching for movement: a few weeks at least, ideally across a season.
safetyNote: Call a licensed structural engineer before any repair if you see: a horizontal crack in a basement or crawl space wall; a wall that bows, leans, or bulges inward; a crack wider than 1/4 inch; one side of a crack sticking out past the other; a crack that grows between checks; a stair-step crack in block or brick that is wider at one end; or cracks along with sticking doors and windows, sloping floors, or a chimney pulling away. An inward bulge of an inch or more in a block or brick wall is serious. Do not dig deep next to a foundation wall yourself: removing soil from one side can let a stressed wall move. Wear eye protection and gloves when you mix epoxy or cement, and keep the space ventilated.
toolsParts: Ruler or crack width card (a US quarter is about 1/16 inch thick)
Pencil or paint marker to date the crack ends
Phone camera for a dated photo log
Crack monitor (optional) to track small movement
Wire brush and shop vacuum to clean the crack
Crack injection kit with surface ports: epoxy for dry, dormant cracks; polyurethane for damp or leaking cracks
Hydraulic cement to plug an active leak
4-foot level or string line to check a wall for bowing
Safety glasses, nitrile gloves, and a dust mask
Downspout extensions, shovel, and rake for drainage and grading

disclaimer: General homeowner guidance, not a substitute for an on-site inspection. Foundation problems vary by soil, climate, and construction; when a crack shows any structural warning sign, have a licensed structural or foundation engineer evaluate it before acting.
